panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows an initial MRI FLAIR scan demonstrating diffuse leukoencephalopathy, consistent with the clinical presentation of West Nile neuroinvasive disease, involving regions characteristic of the pathology. B: Panel B shows a repeat MRI nine months later, demonstrating interval resolution of white matter signal change, which is a recorded clinical course of the disease.

in_text_mentions: He had a repeat MRI brain done three and nine months following his initial presentation, which revealed an interval decrease in abnormal signal change (Figure 4). He also had interval electroencephalogram (EEG) without seizures or epileptiform patterns. His headaches completely resolved, and he did not have any recurrent seizures on an anti-seizure regimen of levetiracetam at his nine-month follow-up visit.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: CT image demonstrating diffuse white matter hypoattenuation in the frontal and parietal regions, consistent with West Nile Encephalitis described in the article. B: CT image demonstrating diffuse white matter hypoattenuation in the frontoparietal and temporal lobes, consistent with West Nile Encephalitis. C: CT image demonstrating diffuse white matter hypoattenuation in the occipital lobes, consistent with West Nile Encephalitis. D: CT image demonstrating diffuse white matter hypoattenuation involving the brain stem and cerebellum, consistent with West Nile Encephalitis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: The panel shows a DWI sequence of a patient with West Nile Neuroinvasive Disease, demonstrating restricted diffusion in the occipital horn, as described in the caption and article text. B: The panel shows the corresponding ADC map of the brain MRI, confirming the punctate lesion (restricted diffusion) seen in West Nile Neuroinvasive Disease.
panels.attribution_text: Kogulan et al. A Multisystem Presentation of West Nile Neuroinvasive Disease: Lessons in Diagnostic Complexity.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.115298. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Repeat brain MRI demonstrating persistent tiny foci of restricted diffusion along the occipital horns of the lateral ventricles, slightly more prominent on the left. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is shown on the left, with the corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map on the right. Red arrows indicate the area of abnormal diffusion.
in_text_mentions: strength grading, deep tendon reflexes, plantar responses, sensory examination, coordination, and gait could not be reliably assessed at that time because of sedation. These components were not subsequently documented in sufficient detail to permit retrospective reporting. Repeat MRI showed a punctate lesion in the occipital horn (Figure 3) that was likely secondary to this patient’s meningoencephalitis. Continued limb weakness was concerning, as it is not a normal finding consistent with meningoencephalitis, though MRI of the cervical spine was negative for any acute spinal cord abnormality.
